I don’t know why it’s taken me so long to get around to playing Hacknet, but now I’m kicking myself for not playing it sooner. I have not felt this engaged in an investigative simulation since I played The Black Watchmen and I really hope to find more games like this.

Hacknet is definitely a game for certain types of people, but you don’t need to have extensive IT experience to play. I think gamers who are already comfortable using command prompt will feel at home with this sim, but the game’s tutorial does a good job of walking you through the concepts and gameplay basics while still leaving you free to get creative with how to implement the tools at your disposal. Nobody is going to learn to be a [i]real[/i] hacker by playing this game, but it’s a fun introduction to the ideas behind the process and it’s immersive enough that you feel like you’re really involved with the story.

Hacknet is at its core a mystery game and your task is to track down what happened to a mysterious person who contacts you. As you work your way across the shadowy world of IP addresses, you are given more abilities and greater challenges to tinker with. I never felt that any of the tasks were impossible -- it was always that I just missed something or overlooked a scan or available command. Fast typists will have a much easier time of playing as there are frequent timers counting down in the guise of tracers.

I absolutely 100% recommend that you pick up the DLC Labyrinths. It pretty much adds an entire game campaign where you get to expand on your skills using new situations. You can play the DLC any time while still keeping your progress with the main game. Seriously, worth the extra few bucks if you can swing it.

I’ve got Hacknet as a gift when I was learning UNIX commands and then bash scripting for work, what probably made me a perfect target player. It got me really hooked on the Linux system, and I found it a great introduction to coding as a whole. 

That said, it’s not a complicated game and no previous coding knowledge is required to play it. The "real" part mostly involves file manipulations and basic SSH usage, while the hacking part  is based on running non-real programs to break into chosen devices and perform said manipulations.

The whole game takes place in an artificial Linux environment that can be modified to a certain degree. It makes the title even more immersive and believable.

However, it’s worth noting that the core gameplay can become a little repetitive after a few hours, not to say "grindy". It’s definitely not for everyone, but the 2-hour refund window is more than enough to determine if it suits you.

First off before I get started on this review, I want it to be kept in mind that this isn't what would be called a conventional review. So if you just want to know my answer: [/b Yes, I recommend this game. It's a super enjoyable indie game if you like the concept or idea hacking.]

Now, why this review isn't conventional comes down to this review: [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/SirPenguin/recommended/365450/] [/url]
First off, it's an amazing review. However I would like to argue the points he made.

[b][i]this is a casual game[/i][/b]

This game is not intended for those that want to learn programming, it's not intended for those that want to write lines of code out and debug and test it...while yes that is more realistic, what would you rather do, play a casual game and be immersed in the story and puzzles, or have to write out lines of code in order to solve the issues in front of you? (Probably spending tedious hours being bored trying to debug your code)

You'd probably prefer to use the commands the game has pre-made for you. The game design was intentional, most people wouldn't want something that get's "taken to the next level"...at least to the point of writing out lines of code by hand. In fact, most people probably won't have coding experience.

The game is a Story rich simulation game. Not a code markup tool. Not a learning game. It's made to be a fun unique puzzle game. So while regardless you'll probably find enjoyment out of the game, don't go into it expecting to find some crazy challenging puzzle that requires you to write out lines of code by hand, developing your own "hacking tools". Expect a fast pace story rich hacking game.

While I respect the points made in the above review, I felt it necessary to explain what you are really going to get out of this game, instead of a false idea of what it really is.

Hacknet was an experience like no other. Its unique gameplay, tense moments and solid storyline got me hooked the moment I got that first message from Bit.

As an introduction to hacking, it does its job, but nothing more. I wouldn't expect anyone to be able to hack the Pentagon after playing this game. However, that does not detract one bit from the overall experience. It has a solid difficulty curve, so even the most computer-illiterate people will not have too much trouble. It is intuitive, and most importantly it is fun. Base game Hacknet provides an amazing 8 hour experience that everyone should check out. Not to mention the soundtrack, which is phenomenal.

With the Labyrinths DLC, Hacknet gets even more content in the form of a new storyline, new programs, new music and new puzzles. There is not much else to say then, the quality is the same, arguably better in the DLC, and I would recommend purchasing the DLC along with the base game.

Finally, there is a reason why I have so many hours in this game. Despite how amazing it is, Hacknet's story is somewhat short being 8 hours long, plus the DLC taking it to around 12 hours. I have played through the entire game plus DLC multiple times, but those never would have taken me to 100+ hours of playtime. No, I'm talking about mod support for the game, Hacknet Extensions. Extensions allows people to create their own storylines, puzzles, campaigns, etc. for other people to play. There are already many extensions to play, and as an active extensions developer myself, I can definitely say they add to the replayability of the game.

A reasonably niche game that I would recommend to anyone who wants to try something different.

review_text_raw:
This game is definitely fun to play, even though it looks fairly basic at first, and probably won't last you more than 8-15 hours (depending on whether you want to do one playthrough or more).

Your role is that of... yourself, hacker extraordinaire—or something, because in the beginning, your character is probably just fiddling around with their computer. Until they receive an e-mail from Bit, late hacker who's posthumously trying to accomplish what they couldn't do when alive. Armed with a couple of commands and utilities, it's time to jump into the game, a game that may turn out to be bigger than you'd think.

Through a series of e-mails and missions, you get introduced gradually to other hackers, become part of hacking groups, and discover what's hiding behind the Bit case. The game is fairly straightforward in that regard (get a mission, hack ports, hack your way in, steal/delete data, delete logs, disconnect), and getting the tools you need isn't hard, however most of the computers you discover along the way also contain other files you can read, such as IRC logs, and part of the fun I had came from exploring. You also have to make a few choices that may affect which missions are available to you—for instance, accepting missions from another hacker will prevent you from taking another hacker's contracts—as well as a couple of other choices about more ethically-challenged assignments.

The interface is simple enough, in a "minimalist OS" way, with a few animations when running hacking utilities; I quite liked that, as seeing more "Holywood hacking animations" wouldn't have been very believable (but not displaying anything would, on the other hand, be a bit boring). I didn't really like the window with nodes representing all the computers you could access, though: it was nice in the beginning, then became seriously cluttered (in the end, I'd just type the IP addresses directly in the terminal, it was faster).

Interestingly, if you've never worked with Unix-based workstations, or Linux, this can actually be a nice little introduction to that kind of OS. Very basic, obviously, with commands that don't even need any arguments; still, since a lot of what you have to do in game is terminal-based, be ready to type fast and work with commands much more than with just clicking on buttons (being used to TABbing my way both in bash and on IOS, I was totally fine with that, and most often I would be faster this way). Getting the hang of this isn't very difficult, and even if you know nothing to running commands, the game will easily make you feel like you do.

Sounds and music: mostly music, with one voiceover at a given point, and alerts when you're getting traced. At first, I feared the audio tracks would become repetitive; in the long run, they fit pretty well, with appropriate change of tracks when you get into a new hacking group or attempt a new kind of operation, and provided good background music without being intrusive.

Problems I noticed: the game runs in full-screen and would crash when I alt-tabbed out of it. Not sure if it's just my computer, or systematic. It didn't detract from my enjoyment, so I admit I didn't pay much attention (and didn't exactly *have to* alt-tab out of it anyway, since the immersion is much better if you don't).

Awaiting the next DLC now? I also wouldn't mind multiplayer possibilities, like hacking each other, or having to form alliances. That would be fun as well.

Conclusion: Recommended.

Wow... I just finished it and especially the Labyrinths DLC (Kaguya trails) was very nice. The original game felt more quicker, whereas in the Kaguya missions, you actually had to dig deeper and make use of your tools in situations where it is not obvious. Both endgames were very nice and adrenalin-rushy and the whole game was accompanied with good music scores who supported the vibe of the missions.

Spoiler alert, but very noteworthy remark about Labyrinth DLC:
[spoiler] There was a unique time in the Labyrinth DLC where the game takes place on your actual computer and the actual windows CMD (and not in the simulated environment!). How cool is that?! I have never seen that before! [/spoiler]

It has been a long time since I really enjoyed a game and I learnt more about hacking too. This game inspired me to go out and look into Grey Hack, which is a bit more realistic than this. However, Hacknet does teach you some core mechanics of hacking and moving around with the bash terminal. The terminal doesn't have many commands though, and some functions are used in a simpler manner like nmap. There is also not a easy way to edit .txt with leafpad or nano. That doesn't exist. So you have to use 'replace list,txt x y' and append. As far as I know there is not even a way to delete a line.

In short: Nice game that teaches some basics about the terminal and hacking, good music, adrenalin rushes, a bit repetitive missions, not many commands available, a bit of a weird ai with the email and netmap, but really fun to have played!

review_text_raw:
[b]What's positive (!)[/b]

Hacknet is an exceptionally atmospheric terminal-driven puzzle game that serves as an engaging introduction to fundamental networking and command-line mechanics. Rather than relying on gamified quick-time events, it requires you to interact directly with a Unix-like environment. Navigating directories, manipulating files, and executing core CLI commands such as ls, cd, cat, and scp quickly becomes second nature. Beyond basic shell operations, the game introduces foundational computer science and infrastructure concepts, forcing you to logically chain exploit tools, scan for open standard ports such as FTP on 21, SSH on 22, and HTTP on 80 and target specific running services to compromise root access.

[b]What's negative (!)[/b]

Its primary shortcoming lies in the user interface during late-game network expansion. As the number of target nodes increases, the graphical Display Map degrades in usability due to dynamic node overlap. Selecting specific server locations on the grid becomes increasingly tedious, making manual network mapping and spatial orientation unnecessarily chaotic in the final chapters.

[b]In conlusion (!) [/b]

Despite the cluttered visual map layout in the late game, the combination of realistic terminal interaction and logical sequence planning makes Hacknet a standout recommendation. As a certified IT specialist, I highly recommend it to both tech enthusiasts and prospective Linux admins alike.

Also, another note, the game is not cringy bad hacking. It way oversimplifies things, but its no "follow the maze to hack the system" kind of thing. The things you 'do' in game are semi-legit.
